source.title: Linear Representation Transferability Hypothesis: Leveraging Small Models to Steer Large Models
source.authors: Femi Bello; Anubrata Das; Fanzhi Zeng; Fangcong Yin; Liu Leqi

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether affine maps transfer representations across model sizes by measuring whether mapped steering vectors preserve their effects; this is a functional test of V4, not a test of convergence with increasing scale using representation-similarity metrics.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates affine transfer within the Gemma-2 family. It does not test a trend of increasing alignment with scale or capability, cross-modal alignment, convergence across random seeds, or recurring interpretable features. Steering behaviors are deliberately induced; the relevant evidence here is whether their effects transfer. The SAE decoder-matrix projection result and steering-transfer outcomes are included. Cited results and speculative implications are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study learns affine maps between Gemma-2-2b and Gemma-2-9b hidden states. It then tests whether transferred steering vectors reproduce native steering effects. That is a functional test of V4 (linear mappability across models). It does not test convergence with scale (V1), cross-modal alignment (V2), seed convergence (V3), interpretable feature recurrence (V5), metric dependence (V6) or causes of convergence (V7). The models share family, tokenizer and similar data, so they are not independently trained in the sense V1 means.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that an affine map can transfer representations between models when training data and architectures are similar. They add that steering vectors from Gemma-2-2b can steer Gemma-2-9b with effect comparable to native vectors, and they present this as evidence for the LRT hypothesis and a shared universal representation space. They explicitly leave limits across larger scale gaps and across model families as open questions.
record.recipe_differences: The study learns affine hidden-state maps and evaluates them through SAE decoder projection and steering transfer; it does not use the original sources' convergence measurements or measure representational similarity increasing with scale.
record.method_sensitivity: The refusal-transfer plots distinguish a chat-mixture mapping dataset from purely pretraining data; the logit-transfer results vary by task, with myopic-reward showing weaker correlation and larger MSE.
record.problems: Evidence is confined to models from one family and two stated sizes, with similar training distributions and a shared tokenizer. The paper does not test whether alignment grows with scale or generalizes across families, architectures, modalities, or seed differences. The refusal result is presented as plots with no numerical curve values in the text; its evaluation uses 15 samples. The logit-transfer task results vary, and myopic-reward is weaker than the others.

untested.parts: No trend with size or capability; only one 2b–9b pair from a single family. The models are not independently trained across architectures, objectives or data.
No vision–language or paired image–caption data.

Only affine maps within the Gemma-2 family with a shared tokenizer. No stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, or cross-family or cross-architecture transfer. There is no direct held-out reconstruction quality with a baseline, and no random-vector or unmapped steering control.
No test of whether the same interpretable SAE features or circuits recur. The decoder projection is a whole-matrix linear fit.
No comparison of similarity metrics, metric settings or OOD inputs.
No test of plateau or completeness, and no manipulation of shared data or objectives.

missing.what: Final validation loss of the learned affine maps (l2l Pile 5.935, l2l mixture 5.986, s2l 5.437). This is a direct measure of mapping loss, though no baseline is given.
s2l vs l2l steering results for capitalization, dog mentions and French (Figure 3), which are not quantified in the text

record.verdict_notes: Evidence comes from a single model pair (Gemma-2-2b→9b, layer 20) with a shared tokenizer and data. The 'Significant' column in Table 1 is not explained. The paper notes that concurrent work (Oozeer et al.) reports mixed or negative results for affine transfer. That is a cited result and is not recorded as a row.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep tests whether alignment increases with model size or capability, nor does it compare independently trained models across architectures, objectives, data, or modalities.
No paired image-caption vision-language representations are tested.
No models with the same architecture but different initializations are compared for shared features or subspaces.

Tests affine transfer within the Gemma-2 family, primarily through transferred steering effects. It does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired-data mappings, or broad cross-family transfer.
The SAE decoder matrices are compared by linear projection error, but the study does not test whether the same interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
No comparison of similarity metrics, metric settings, or in-distribution versus out-of-distribution inputs.

The study uses models from one family and similar training distributions; it does not vary shared data or objectives to test their causal contribution, nor assess whether alignment plateaus or remains incomplete.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b SAE decoder (projected from Gemma-2-9b SAE decoder)
rows.operation_detail: Least-squares linear projection of the Gemma-2-9b SAE decoder matrix onto the Gemma-2-2b decoder matrix
rows.measure: Frobenius-norm reconstruction error of the projected decoder matrix
rows.value: around 114; authors describe the average reconstruction error per entry as small
rows.note: The paper reports the result for the decoder-matrix pair and interprets it as evidence that the feature matrices are approximately linearly related.
rows.check: Baseline is not 'not stated': the comparison is the random-matrix projection (r2). The text gives one number (Frobenius ≈114) and calls the per-entry error small. The least-squares fit assumes SAE feature indices are aligned across models (R_S=R_T=I), which Gemma Scope SAEs do not guarantee, so this is weak evidence. The figure reference in the text is broken ('Figure ??').

rows.subject: Random matrices with the same dimensions as the Gemma-2-9b and Gemma-2-2b decoder matrices
rows.size_stated: same dimensions as the decoder matrices
rows.operation_detail: Project random matrices using the same procedure as for the SAE decoder matrices
rows.value: figure only; text states the errors are significantly larger
rows.note: The text gives no numerical random-matrix error.
rows.check: This is a control for r1, not an independent result. Its baseline should read 'Gemma decoder projection error (≈114)'. There is no numeric random-matrix error, only 'significantly larger'.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-9b
rows.operation_detail: Compare steering with SAE feature coefficients mapped to target hidden states (s2l) against steering with mapped source hidden states (l2l)
rows.measure: Preservation of the steering vector's semantic effect
rows.value: The paper states that s2l steering is more effective than l2l steering
rows.note: The result is reported jointly for the listed steering behaviors, without separate numerical outcomes.
rows.check: Compares two of the study's own mapping variants (s2l vs l2l), not transferred against native steering. No numbers or per-behaviour outcomes are reported, and Figure 3 is not quantified in the text. It cannot show how much is lost by the mapping.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b and Gemma-2-9b (transfer pair; direction not specified for each curve)
rows.operation_detail: Transfer a CAA refusal-removal steering vector between models and sweep steering strength
rows.measure: Mean refusal score over steering strengths α
rows.value: figure only; authors state the transferred vector has the same effect as one learned natively
rows.uncertainty: Error estimates shown; text describes them as estimates from sampling but gives no numerical values
rows.note: The paper states this result holds whether the steering vector was learned on Gemma-2-2b or Gemma-2-9b; exact curve values and transfer directions are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Figure-only; the state rests on the authors' statement that the effect matches native steering. Uses a GPT-4.1 binary harmlessness judge and 15 samples per α. Table 2 lists only 2b→9b maps, yet the text claims the result also holds for vectors learned on 9b; the transfer direction is unclear. This mapping uses the instruction-tuned (-it) models.

rows.operation_detail: Transfer a CAA refusal-removal steering vector between models and sweep steering strength
rows.measure: Mean refusal score over steering strengths α
rows.value: figure only; authors state the transferred vector has the same effect as one learned natively
rows.uncertainty: Error estimates shown; text describes them as estimates from sampling but gives no numerical values
rows.note: The paper states this result holds whether the steering vector was learned on Gemma-2-2b or Gemma-2-9b; exact curve values and transfer directions are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Same caveats as r4 (figure-only, GPT-4.1 judge, 15 samples, unclear direction). Uses the Pile-trained map.

relationships.condition: Logit-based (Tan et al.) steering transfer 2b→9b, 12 of 13 tasks
relationships.reason: Transferred and native steering propensities correlate 0.807–0.981, with MSE between 5.2e-03 and 4.9e-02 (r6–r21, r24–r31).
relationships.display_finding: Transferred and native steering propensities correlated 0.807–0.981 across 12 of 13 tasks, with MSE 5.2e-03–4.9e-02.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Logit-based (Tan et al.) steering transfer 2b→9b, 12 of 13 tasks
source_check.reason: Section 3.4 and Table 1 report correlations 0.807–0.981 and low MSE for these tasks, supporting preservation of selected steering effects through an affine map.

relationships.reason: Transfer is notably weaker and noisier here: correlation 0.728±0.344 and MSE 9.56e-02±1.16e-01 (r22, r23).
relationships.display_finding: Transfer yielded correlation 0.728±0.344 and mean squared error 9.56×10⁻²±1.16×10⁻¹, indicating weaker and more variable mapping.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Table 1 reports the lowest correlation, 0.728 ± 0.344, and highest mean MSE, 9.56e-02 ± 1.16e-01. Transfer remains significant but is weaker and more variable.

relationships.condition: Refusal-removal steering transfer, chat-mixture and Pile maps

relationships.display_finding: The authors reported that transferred vectors matched native refusal removal in an evaluation using a GPT-4.1 judge and 15 samples.
